stem: Infusion of 40ml/kg of 0.9% saline solution will cause:
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

A 40 mL/kg infusion is a large saline load. 0.9% saline contains sodium and chloride at 154 mmol/L, so it delivers chloride well above the normal plasma concentration. Plasma chloride therefore rises proportionately more than sodium, reducing the plasma strong ion difference and increasing hydrogen ion concentration. The resulting fall in pH is a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, typically with a normal anion gap.

Source: Anesthetic Pharmacology (Evers), p. 804; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 677; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 685

stem: Buffering of a bicarbonate infusion:

options.B: Is exchanged for Cl- across the red cell membrane
options.C: Is compensated for by an increased respiratory rate
options.E: Is buffered predominantly by bone carbonate stores

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Bicarbonate crosses the erythrocyte membrane through band 3, the bicarbonate/chloride exchanger; reciprocal movement of Cl− maintains electrochemical neutrality. Thus infused HCO3− is exchanged for Cl− across the red cell membrane. The respiratory response is not an increased rate: compensation for alkalosis involves decreased ventilation, which retains CO2 and increases extracellular H+.

Source: Nunn & Lumb's Respiratory Physiology, p. 158; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 682; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 391

stem: Phosphate buffer system is an effective buffer intracellularly and in renal tubules because:

options.E: It functions as a closed buffer system

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

The phosphate buffer system has a pK of 6.8, close to the lower pH of renal tubular and intracellular fluid, so it operates near its maximum buffering power. Phosphate becomes greatly concentrated in renal tubular fluid and is present at a much higher concentration intracellularly than extracellularly. Thus A, B and C are all correct, making D the keyed answer.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 391; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 621

stem: Metabolic acidosis is characterised by:
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Metabolic acidosis produces acidemia, increasing extracellular [H+]. Hydrogen ions enter cells and are buffered intracellularly, thereby increasing intracellular [H+]. The primary extracellular change is reduced bicarbonate, but this may result from bicarbonate loss or buffering of added acid, not necessarily decreased bicarbonate production. Respiratory compensation increases ventilation and lowers PaCO2. The anion gap may be either normal, as in hyperchloremic acidosis, or increased, as in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis.

Source: Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 685; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 403

stem: Bicarbonate system is the most important ECF buffer system because:

options.A: It has a pKa close to physiological pH
options.B: Haemoglobin is only present in red blood cells
options.C: HCO3- occurs in such large amounts
options.D: It is present in high concentration inside red blood cells
options.E: CO2 can be regulated by the lung and HCO3- by the kidneys

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

The bicarbonate system is the most important extracellular buffer because its components are regulated independently: CO2 is rapidly regulated by pulmonary ventilation, while HCO3− is regulated by renal reabsorption and excretion. This makes it an open physiological buffer system with substantial effective capacity. Its pKa is 6.1, well below physiological pH 7.4, so proximity of pKa to physiological pH is not the reason.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 307; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 681; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 390

stem: During infusion of an acidic solution (hydrochloric acid solution), which contributes most to buffering?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Hydrochloric acid is a strong, non-carbonic acid. In extracellular fluid, H+ is buffered predominantly by bicarbonate: HCl + NaHCO3 forms H2CO3 + NaCl, converting a strong acid to weak carbonic acid. Bicarbonate is the chief plasma buffer at 24 mmol/L and buffers approximately 70% of non-carbonic acids. Phosphate has a minor extracellular role because its concentration is low. Intracellular proteins have substantial capacity, but maximal buffering of extracellular acid–base disturbances is delayed for several hours.

Source: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 622; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 308; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 391

stem: In a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis, the following are true except:

options.A: There is an increased anion gap
options.C: There is decreased concentration of H+ intracellularly
options.D: Renal excretion of titratable acids will be increased
options.E: There is increased synthesis of bicarbonate

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is an increased-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The increased extracellular H+ concentration promotes movement of H+ into cells, so intracellular H+ concentration increases, not decreases; therefore C is false. Respiratory compensation increases ventilation and lowers PaCO2. Renal compensation increases H+ excretion as titratable acid and NH4+, while adding newly generated HCO3− to the extracellular fluid.

Chloride concentration increases to maintain electroneutrality as bicarbonate falls, so the anion gap remains normal and the acidosis is hyperchloraemic. Thus, the most likely disorder is hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.

stem: During infusion of hydrochloric acid (HCl), which contributes most to buffering? (repeated MCQ)
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Infused HCl is a strong, non-carbonic acid that dissociates to release H+. In extracellular fluid, H+ is buffered predominantly by bicarbonate: H+ combines with HCO3−, forming H2CO3 and then CO2 and H2O. Bicarbonate is the chief plasma buffer at approximately 24 mmol/L and buffers about 70% of non-carbonic acids. Phosphate contributes little because its extracellular concentration is low; intracellular protein buffering is slower to become maximally effective.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 308; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 390; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 391; Vander's Renal Physiology, p. 156

stem: Severe hypercapnia is most likely to be associated with:
reason:

Hypercapnia and its associated acidosis stimulate catecholamine release and sympathetic cardiovascular effects, so increased catecholamines are expected. Although sympathetic stimulation may increase cardiac output, the direct effect of elevated Pco2 on myocardial contractility is depressant, making increased myocardial contractility an inappropriate alternative. Hypercapnic acidosis also causes potassium to move from cells into plasma, rather than decreasing plasma potassium.

Source: Nunn & Lumb's Respiratory Physiology, p. 328; Nunn & Lumb's Respiratory Physiology, p. 331

stem: The H+ production by body metabolism that has to be excreted by the kidney to prevent acidosis is:

Because H+ is monovalent, 80 mEq equals 80 mmol; among the options, 68 mmol is the appropriate value and order of magnitude. The much larger volatile acid load, approximately 15,000 mmol/day as CO2, is eliminated by the lungs.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 394; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 305

Hypertension is an unreliable clinical sign: sympathetic stimulation often produces a small rise in blood pressure, but the response is variable. Hypokalaemia is incorrect because hypercapnic acidosis causes potassium ions to move from cells into plasma, increasing plasma potassium.

stem: Which of the following is a 'strong ion'?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

In Stewart’s physicochemical approach, strong ions are produced by electrolytes that dissociate completely in solution. Chloride (Cl−) is specifically classified as a strong ion. In contrast, bicarbonate, phosphate and albumin are weak ions because their parent electrolytes dissociate only partially and participate in buffering.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 318; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 621

A pKa of 7.4 is not a defining feature of strong ions; pKa describes acid dissociation. Phosphate is a weak ion because it only partially dissociates in solution.

Source: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 621; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 318

Magnesium, calcium and chloride are strong ions, and lactate is included among the strong anions contributing to the apparent strong ion difference. Bicarbonate is not a strong ion: it is produced by a weak electrolyte system and is a dependent variable determined by the independent variables SID, Atot and PCO2.

stem: A 19 year old is admitted unconscious with arterial blood gases: PaO2 117, PaCO2 26, pH 7.1, base excess -15. This is most consistent with:

PaCO2 is reduced at 26 mmHg, below the normal range of 35–45 mmHg, because metabolic acidosis stimulates alveolar ventilation and thereby removes carbon dioxide. This is respiratory compensation, which is generally incomplete, so the pH remains below normal. Metabolic acidosis without compensation would not explain the reduced PaCO2.

Source: West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 110; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 687; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 627

stem: Base excess calculation:

Question text repaired in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Muscle efficiency is the percentage of nutrient chemical-energy input converted into external work rather than heat. Even under optimal conditions, skeletal muscle converts less than 25% into work, so the approximate maximum is 25%. About half the energy in foodstuffs is lost during ATP formation, and only 40% to 45% of ATP energy is subsequently converted into work. Maximum efficiency occurs at a moderate contraction velocity, about 30% of maximum.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 85

stem: The immediate energy source used by the contractile proteins of muscle is:

stem: Cardiac muscle is different from skeletal muscle because of:
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Cardiac muscle depends on Ca2+ influx through slowly opening L-type calcium channels, which remain open for 200–300 ms and contribute to the prolonged action-potential plateau. This entering Ca2+ activates ryanodine receptors, producing calcium-triggered calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. In skeletal muscle, ryanodine receptors are activated predominantly by voltage-dependent physical coupling to dihydropyridine receptors. Fast Na+ channels and actin–myosin interaction occur in both muscle types, so they do not distinguish cardiac muscle.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 105; Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, p. 69

Intrafusal fibres are specialised striated muscle fibres. Their polar regions contain contractile elements and are innervated by γ motor fibres; contraction of these regions stretches the largely non-contractile central sensory region. The muscle spindle detects muscle length and its rate of change, whereas tension is detected by Golgi tendon organs. Therefore, intrafusal fibres contain contractile elements, making C correct.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 105; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 649

stem: Skeletal muscle action potential:

options.D: Sodium channels remain open throughout repolarisation

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Depolarization activates voltage-gated K+ channels more slowly than voltage-gated Na+ channels. Thus delayed rectifier K+ current begins before peak depolarisation and K+ efflux subsequently drives repolarisation as Na+ channels inactivate. Skeletal muscle resting membrane potential is approximately −90 mV, not −80 or −55 mV. Approximately −55 mV is the threshold for activation of fast Na+ channels, not −30 mV, and these channels become inactivated during repolarisation.

stem: Which is incorrect regarding the Krebs cycle:

options.A: Acetyl-CoA is metabolised to CO2 & H+
options.E: Cycle is continuous during anaerobic metabolism but at a slower rate

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

E is incorrect. The Krebs cycle operates only under aerobic conditions because the electron transport chain is required to regenerate NAD+ and FAD. Without oxygen, oxidative phosphorylation ceases, NADH accumulates and the cycle stops. Anaerobic glycolysis can continue by reducing pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+; the Krebs cycle does not merely continue more slowly. Using classic accounting, each acetyl-CoA yields three NADH, one FADH2 and one ATP, equivalent to 12 ATP.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 426; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 430

Fat oxidation produces the lowest RQ, approximately 0.7, compared with 1.0 for carbohydrate, so increased fat metabolism explains a low RQ. stem: Lactate:

options.A: Is the way products of glucose enter the citric acid cycle
options.B: Formation is used to regenerate NADP
options.C: Is the substrate produced to enter the citric acid cycle

options.E: Is converted directly to acetyl-CoA in muscle

reason:

Normal resting plasma lactate is approximately 0.5–2 mmol/L because lactate is continually produced by physiological anaerobic glycolysis, particularly in red blood cells, which lack mitochondrial respiratory enzymes. During anaerobic glycolysis, pyruvate accepts hydrogen from NADH + H+ to form lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Pyruvate, not lactate, enters mitochondria and forms acetyl CoA for the citric acid cycle; lactate formation regenerates NAD+, not NADP.

stem: Phosphorylase:

options.A: Is found in all human cells
options.D: In liver increases glycogen production and reduces breakdown of glycogen
options.E: Is activated by insulin via cAMP

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Glycogen phosphorylase is present in liver and muscle, where it mediates glycogenolysis. It catalyses phosphorolytic breakdown of glycogen, releasing glucose-1-phosphate. In both tissues, inactive phosphorylase b is converted to active phosphorylase a. Epinephrine activates, rather than inhibits, glycogen phosphorylase. Insulin has the opposite effect: it inactivates liver phosphorylase, reduces glycogenolysis and promotes glycogen synthesis through glycogen synthase.

Source: Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 738; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 399

stem: Creatine phosphate:

options.A: Is a source of creatinine for protein synthesis
options.B: Is a source of cyclic AMP for second messenger systems
options.C: Is a high-energy phosphate source for muscle contraction

Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Creatine phosphate, or phosphocreatine, contains a high-energy phosphate bond and acts as an immediate energy reserve in muscle. It donates phosphate to ADP via creatine phosphokinase, rapidly regenerating ATP. ATP then supplies the energy used directly by the contractile proteins. Thus, creatine phosphate is a high-energy phosphate source supporting muscle contraction, particularly during brief, maximal activity.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 85; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 99; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 848

stem: Metabolic rate is increased least with:
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

A hot climate increases metabolic rate least; climatic adaptation reduces thyroid secretion, and people in tropical regions have a basal metabolic rate about 10% lower than those in temperate climates. By contrast, exercise markedly increases energy expenditure, food produces diet-induced thermogenesis, and cold stimulates shivering and sympathetic nonshivering thermogenesis. Increased central nervous system activity also raises metabolic rate, whereas reduced central nervous system activity during sleep contributes to a 10% to 15% decrease.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 851; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 852; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 437

stem: Factors causing quickest rise in metabolic rate:
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Skeletal muscle activity causes the quickest and most dramatic rise in metabolic rate. Cellular activity converts ATP to ADP; the increased ADP concentration accelerates oxidative metabolic pathways in proportion to activity. Maximal whole-body muscle exercise can increase heat production to about 50 times normal for a few seconds. In contrast, after a high-protein meal, metabolic rate begins rising within an hour and reaches a maximum of about 30% above normal.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 850; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 852

stem: What has the greatest immediate effect on metabolic rate?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Skeletal muscle activity produces the greatest immediate change in metabolic rate. Muscle contraction rapidly converts ATP to ADP, accelerating oxidative pathways and energy release. Maximal whole-body muscle exercise can increase heat production to about 50 times normal for a few seconds, or about 20 times normal during sustained exercise in a well-trained person. Renal tubular ion transport consumes substantial ATP, but does not produce a comparable immediate increase in whole-body metabolic rate.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 850; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 852; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 695

Whole-body metabolic rate is least altered by mental activity. Skeletal muscle activity can increase whole-body heat production up to 50-fold briefly; catecholamine release increases metabolic activity and heat generation; and cold activates shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis. Heat exposure above the upper critical temperature is not necessarily metabolically neutral because active heat-loss responses are required, so D is not reliably the least change. stem: In a resting patient at metabolic steady state, which of the following would predictably increase the cellular respiratory quotient by changing the predominant oxidised substrate?

Cellular respiratory quotient is determined by the predominant oxidised substrate: carbohydrate has an RQ of 1.0, whereas fat has an RQ of about 0.7. Low-lipid, high-carbohydrate total parenteral nutrition therefore shifts substrate oxidation toward carbohydrate and increases steady-state cellular RQ toward 1.0. By contrast, strenuous exercise may raise the measured respiratory exchange ratio above 1 because lactic acidosis increases ventilation; this does not represent a substrate cellular RQ above 1.

stem: For two solutions separated by a semi-permeable membrane (Solution A: saline solution AND solution B: H2O): Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: A hydrostatic pressure applied to A will stop osmotic pressure
options.B: There will be bulk flow from A to B
options.C: The fluid level in B will go up
options.D: The NaCl concentration at A will remain the same

Solution A has a lower water concentration than pure water in solution B because dissolved NaCl displaces water. Water therefore moves from B to A by osmosis, raising the level in A and diluting its NaCl. Applying sufficient hydrostatic pressure to A opposes this movement; the pressure required to stop osmosis is the osmotic pressure of the NaCl solution. Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Transferrin carries plasma iron and is normally about 30% saturated. In iron deficiency, reduced available iron means that a smaller proportion of transferrin iron-binding sites is occupied, so transferrin saturation decreases. Iron stores are also depleted, with decreased plasma ferritin and absent reticuloendothelial haemosiderin; therefore increased ferritin or haemosiderin is incorrect.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 328; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 459

The body has no means of actively excreting iron, so iron balance is regulated mainly by intestinal absorption. Iron loss occurs predominantly through sloughing of ferritin-containing intestinal mucosal cells. Smaller amounts are lost in bile, sweat and urine; therefore, renal excretion is not the major route. Renal peritubular interstitial cells respond by increasing erythropoietin production, which stimulates red cell precursor proliferation and maturation. stem: Lignocaine works by:
reason:

- Main mechanism of action: Antagonism of VG-Na+ channels in excitable tissues
o Unionised LA diffuses across the phospholipid membrane into the more acidic axoplasm and then becomes ionized → Ionised LA binds to the inner portion of the channel (H- or internal-gate of α-subunit) from within the cell (but can also obstruct the channel physically at its external opening)
o LA binding to the channel is dependent on its conformational state → LAs have a high affinity for binding to the channel in its activated-open and inactivated- closed states:
 (i) LA gains access to its binding site within the channel ONLY it is in its activated open state during an AP
 (ii) LA then preferentially binds the channel during in inactivated-closed state and stabilises it in this conformation → Maintains channel in inactivated-closed state, and prevents reversion back to rested-closed state and activated-open state
o Antagonism of VG-Na+ channels results in ↓ Na+ permeability and flow across the membrane → This (i) slows the rate of rise in membrane depolarisation, and (ii) lowers the magnitude of membrane depolarisation → Produces two effects:
 VTHRESHOLD is met (Ie. lower [LA]) – AP is still generated but will have a slower impulse conduction (Ie. decreased slope of phase 0 of AP)
 VTHRESHOLD is not met (Ie. sufficient [LA]) – AP is not generated and impulse propagation is prevented (“conduction blockade”)
Note: The RMP and Level of VTHRESHOLD are NOT altered!
o LAs demonstrate “Frequency-dependent blockade”:
 A nerve that is repeatedly stimulated (Ie. ↑ frequency AP generated) is MORE sensitive to LA-induced conduction blockade than a nerve at rest
 This is because LA can only gain access to its binding site within the VG- Na+ channel to exert its effect when the channel is in an activated-open state during an AP
- Alternate mechanisms of action:
 Note: "Membrane expansion theory" is an alternate mechanism – Unionized lipid soluble LA dissolves into the phospholipid membrane and causes swelling of the lipoprotein matrix → Leads to disruption/inactivation of VG-Na+ channel
o (a) Antagonise other VG channels (VG-K+ channels and L-type Ca2+ channels), but with lower affinity than VG-Na+ channels
o (b) Also act on GPCRs

Brown-fat thermogenesis is autonomically mediated. Cold exposure increases sympathetic activity; norepinephrine released from sympathetic nerve endings activates β3-receptors, promoting lipolysis and heat production. options.A: The anterior and posterior spinal arteries do not anastomose with each other within the spinal cord
options.B: Radicular arteries enter the vertebral canal only between T10 and L1
options.C: Radicular arteries enter the vertebral canal through the laminar foramina
options.D: The anterior spinal artery travels on the right side of the spinal cord
options.E: The anterior spinal artery supplies the posterior one-third of the spinal cord

reason:
Question text repaired in the tracker's curated copy, 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

The anterior and posterior spinal arteries do not anastomose with each other within the spinal cord. The anterior spinal artery is a midline vessel in the anterior median fissure and supplies the anterior two-thirds, whereas the posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior one-third. Radicular arteries accompany the ventral and dorsal nerve roots through the intervertebral foramina and occur at multiple spinal levels, not only between T10 and L1.

Source: Anatomy for Anaesthetists, p. 162; Anatomy for Anaesthetists, p. 159; Cousins & Bridenbaugh Neural Blockade, p. 227

section: CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW, INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE & SPINAL CORD PERFUSION
stem: With regard to cerebral blood flow

options.A: Increased blood flow occurs with increased neuronal activity
options.B: It depends on MAP and ICP alone
options.C: It increases with increased plasma glucose level
options.D: It is directly proportional to arterial oxygen content
options.E: It decreases with increased cerebral metabolic rate

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Cerebral blood flow is coupled to cerebral metabolism. Increased neuronal activity increases local metabolic demand and releases vasoactive mediators, producing arteriolar vasodilatation and an immediate increase in regional cerebral blood flow. For example, hand movement increases flow in the contralateral motor cortex, while visual stimulation increases occipital flow. Therefore A is correct. Option E is the opposite of normal flow–metabolism coupling: cerebral blood flow increases, rather than decreases, as cerebral metabolic rate increases.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 737; Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 64; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 244

section: CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW, INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE & SPINAL CORD PERFUSION
stem: Cerebral blood flow regulation is most affected by
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

PaCO2 is a powerful physiological regulator of cerebral blood flow. At normal arterial pressure, CBF changes almost linearly with PaCO2 from 20 to 80 mmHg, increasing by about 2–4% per 1 mmHg rise. CO2 rapidly crosses the blood–brain barrier, increases extracellular H+ concentration and causes cerebral vasodilatation. In contrast, PaO2 affects CBF mainly below 50 mmHg, while changes in mean arterial pressure are buffered by autoregulation over approximately 50–150 mmHg.

Source: Principles of Physiology for the Anaesthetist (Kam & Power), p. 64; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 246

section: CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW, INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE & SPINAL CORD PERFUSION
stem: Cerebral metabolic rate is

options.B: Decreased equally by volatile and intravenous anaesthetics
options.C: Inversely related to cerebral blood flow
options.D: Not altered by elevated core body temperature

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Cerebral metabolic rate is directly related to neuronal activity. Activation metabolism supplies the energy required for neuronal activity and synaptic transmission; during high brain activity, neuronal metabolism may increase by 100%–150%, largely to restore transmembrane ionic gradients. Cerebral blood flow is coupled directly, not inversely, to metabolic demand. Temperature also affects metabolism: CMRO2 decreases by about 7% for each 1°C decrease in body temperature. Anaesthetic effects on CMRO2 are not uniform.

Source: Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 243; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 244; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 246; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 742

stem: Shivering that is mediated by the hypothalamus:

options.A: Increases muscle tone via muscle spindle feedback
options.B: Is mediated via the red nucleus
options.C: Occurs by rhythmic stimulation of anterior horn cells
options.D: Occurs by activation of a shivering centre in the brainstem
options.E: Is coordinated primarily by the cerebellum

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

The primary motor centre for shivering is in the dorsomedial posterior hypothalamus. It sends nonrhythmic signals through bilateral descending tracts to anterior motor neurons, increasing skeletal muscle tone. Once tone exceeds a critical level, muscle-spindle stretch-reflex feedback oscillations produce shivering. Thus A is correct. The signals themselves are not rhythmic, so C is incorrect; D is also incorrect because the centre is hypothalamic, although its descending pathways traverse the brainstem.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 859; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 860

stem: Transection of a motor nerve leads to:

options.B: Depolarisation of the resting membrane potential

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Motor nerve transection causes axonal denervation of the supplied skeletal muscle. Denervated muscle develops spontaneous electrical activity, including fibrillation potentials, so spontaneous muscle activity is increased. Denervation also causes rapid muscle atrophy because contractile signals required to maintain normal muscle size are lost; therefore, muscle fibre hypertrophy and preservation of muscle mass are incorrect.

Source: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 59; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 89

stem: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF):

options.C: Is produced by choroidal blood vessels and ependymal cells
options.D: Has a composition similar to plasma

CSF is produced mainly by the choroid plexuses, which are vascular structures covered by epithelial cells, with additional production by the ependymal lining; therefore C is correct. Formation is approximately 0.35–0.40 mL/min (500–600 mL/day), and adult CSF volume is about 150 mL. Its ionic, glucose and protein composition differs from plasma. stem: What is true regarding nerve action potentials?

options.B: Potassium efflux begins prior to maximum depolarisation
options.C: Sodium channels return to the resting state at -30 mV
options.D: Potassium channels have resting, activated, and inactivated states
options.E: Potassium channels undergo a 500-1000-fold change in conductance with repolarisation

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Voltage-gated K+ channels are activated by depolarisation, but open more slowly than Na+ channels. Their conductance therefore begins to rise during the upstroke, before peak depolarisation, producing outward K+ current; full activation occurs later and contributes chiefly to repolarisation. Thus K+ efflux begins prior to maximum depolarisation. In contrast, Na+ channels activate at about −55 mV, not −80 mV, and delayed-rectifier K+ channels do not inactivate appreciably.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 68; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 69; Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, p. 63; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 225

Capsaicin activates TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) channels on nociceptive sensory nerve terminals. stem: One mg of alfentanil is administered to a pregnant woman at term for induction of anaesthesia prior to a caesarean section. What percentage of unionised drug (of alfentanil) will be present in the fetal blood?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Alfentanil is a weak base with a pKa of approximately 6.5. At a fetal blood pH of 7.25, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives an unionised-to-ionised ratio of 10^(7.25−6.5) = 5.62. The unionised fraction is therefore 5.62/(1 + 5.62) = 0.85, or approximately 85%; the closest option is 90%. The administered dose, uterine blood flow and extent of placental transfer affect the amount present, not the percentage of alfentanil in fetal blood that is unionised.

Source: Cousins & Bridenbaugh Neural Blockade, p. 560; Anesthetic Pharmacology (Evers), p. 949

Glucose uptake occurs in the proximal tubule via sodium–glucose symporters, driven indirectly by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase, so it is secondary active rather than passive. Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Normal saline contains equal concentrations of the strong cation Na+ and strong anion Cl−: 154 mEq/L each. Therefore, SID = [Na+] − [Cl−] = 154 − 154 = 0 mEq/L. A value near 40–44 mEq/L is the normal plasma SIDa, not the SID of saline itself (Kam & Power, p.318; Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.625).

stem: What is true about vecuronium?

options.B: It is eliminated exclusively by the kidneys and has no active metabolites
options.C: Its neuromuscular block can be reversed with neostigmine
options.E: It is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Vecuronium is a steroidal, intermediate-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Its block can be reversed with neostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Vecuronium is deacetylated to active metabolites and eliminated by hepatic and renal mechanisms. It does not undergo Hofmann elimination, which is characteristic of atracurium and cisatracurium.

Source: Anesthetic Pharmacology (Evers), p. 644; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 432

stem: What is the purpose of egg lecithin in propofol?
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Propofol is highly lipid-soluble and insoluble in water, so it is formulated as an oil-in-water emulsion. Egg lecithin, present as 1.2% purified egg phospholipid, acts as the emulsifier, stabilising the soybean oil and aqueous phases. Soybean oil is the lipid vector, whereas glycerol adjusts tonicity and sodium hydroxide adjusts pH (Evers, p.443).

stem: Action of fibrin in coagulation

options.D: Initiates vasoconstriction at the site of injury
options.E: Provides a phospholipid surface for coagulation factors

Fibrin binds platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors, facilitating linkage of platelets to one another and stabilising the platelet plug (Evers, p.911). It forms threads that attach tightly to platelets and reinforce the plug. Platelet attachment to damaged subendothelium is mediated mainly by collagen and von Willebrand factor, while platelet activation and granule release are induced by agonists such as thrombin, not by fibrin.

stem: What information do A-beta nerve fibres convey
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Aβ fibres are large, myelinated sensory afferents conducting at approximately 30–70 m/s. They innervate cutaneous mechanoreceptors, including Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs, Pacinian corpuscles and Ruffini endings, and convey light touch and pressure. Pain and temperature are principally conveyed by smaller Aδ and C fibres (Cousins & Bridenbaugh, p.56; Guyton & Hall, p.571).

stem: What does NOT worsen paracetamol toxicity
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Acute alcohol intoxication does not worsen paracetamol toxicity while ethanol is present. Ethanol competes with paracetamol for cytochrome P450 2E1, diminishing formation of the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). In contrast, chronic alcohol use induces P450 enzymes and increases toxicity. After alcohol cessation, NAPQI formation may be enhanced over the next 24 hours, increasing hepatic injury (Foundations of Anesthesia, p.733).

stem: A wash-in curve (FA/FI against time over 30 minutes) is shown for 70% nitrous oxide, labelled A. Which curve would be the wash-in for 10% nitrous oxide? [Figure: the top curve, labelled A, rises rapidly to a plateau near 1.0. Three further curves below it plateau at about 0.88 (B), 0.53 (C) and 0.15 (D; labelled A again in the original).]
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Nitrous oxide uptake is a wash-in process (Nunn & Lumb, p.537). At an inspired concentration of 70%, rapid uptake produces a substantial concentration effect, accelerating the rise of FA/FI and giving curve A. At 10%, this effect is smaller, so FA/FI rises more slowly, corresponding to curve B. Curve A is not expected because the blood–gas partition coefficient of nitrous oxide is unchanged by reducing its inspired concentration.

stem: Which of the following is NOT true regarding nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
reason:
Explanation written and 2 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are rapidly acting, excitatory ligand-gated ion channels, not slow inhibitory channels. Acetylcholine binding opens a cation-selective pore, permitting mainly Na+ and K+, and sometimes Ca2+, flux over milliseconds. Each receptor is a pentamer, with the M2 segment of each subunit contributing to the pore. Thus “slow inhibitory/inactive gate” is not a correct description (Rang & Dale’s Pharmacology, p.34; Evers, p.51).

stem: What is NOT an ideal property of an anaesthetic agent when using TIVA
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Zero-order elimination occurs when metabolic capacity is saturated, so a constant amount, rather than a constant fraction, is eliminated per unit time. Elimination is then not proportional to concentration, favouring accumulation during infusion and an unpredictable offset; it is therefore undesirable for TIVA. First-order elimination, with a constant clearance and elimination rate proportional to concentration, is preferable. In contrast, a large ke0 produces rapid plasma–effect-site equilibration, while high clearance, inactive metabolites and a short context-sensitive half-time favour prompt, predictable recovery.

Source: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 30; Anesthetic Pharmacology (Evers), p. 74; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 43; Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 292; Anesthetic Pharmacology (Evers), p. 455

Its distribution half-life is much shorter, approximately 6 minutes, and should not be confused with the terminal elimination phase. Dexmedetomidine is extensively metabolised in the liver. stem: Which of the following is most likely to cause bronchospasm

Desflurane-associated bronchoconstriction is particularly likely in smokers. Sevoflurane instead produces moderate bronchodilation, while isoflurane is irritating but generally bronchodilates. stem: Ratio of blood flow to liver by the hepatic artery vs portal vein
reason:

The hepatic artery supplies approximately 25% of total hepatic blood flow, while the portal vein supplies approximately 75%. Therefore, the ratio of hepatic arterial to portal venous blood flow is 25:75, which simplifies to 1:3. Despite its lower flow contribution, the hepatic artery provides 45%–50% of hepatic oxygen requirements because its blood is highly oxygenated (Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.682).

stem: In what cells does anaerobic respiration normally occur
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Mature erythrocytes rely exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis because they lack mitochondria and therefore lack the mitochondrial respiratory enzymes required for aerobic energy production. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, converts glucose to lactate and yields only two ATP molecules per glucose. It is the only source of energy available to red blood cells (Nunn & Lumb, p.198).

stem: Where is the sensory neuron cell body located?
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

The cell body of a peripheral sensory neuron is located in the dorsal root ganglion. Its peripheral process receives sensory input, while its central process enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root and synapses with second-order neurons in the dorsal horn. Thus, the dorsal horn contains interneurons and second-order sensory neurons, not the cell bodies of primary sensory neurons (Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 78).

Guyton & Hall (p.548) classifies glycine among the amino-acid transmitters, whereas serotonin and dopamine are amines and acetylcholine is classified separately.

stem: At 37°C, what is the Nernst potential for Na+ (inside relative to outside) when the extracellular and intracellular Na+ concentrations are 145 mmol/L and 10 mmol/L, respectively?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

At 37°C, the Nernst equation for a monovalent cation is E = 61 log10([ion]outside/[ion]inside) mV. Therefore, ENa = 61 log10(145/10) = 61 × 1.161 = +70.8 mV, approximately +71 mV. The positive sign indicates that the inside is positive relative to the outside.

Source: Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 222; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 63

stem: Why is carbon monoxide (CO) ideal for use when measuring diffusion capacity?

options.A: Alveolar and arterial concentrations of CO equilibrate rapidly
options.B: Hb rapidly binds to CO in preference to O2
options.C: Minimal uptake of CO from lung
options.E: CO diffuses across the blood-gas barrier much faster than O2

reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

CO has such high affinity for haemoglobin that its partial pressure in pulmonary capillary blood, and hence arterial blood during low-concentration testing, remains effectively zero. Thus the driving pressure can be taken as alveolar PCO, simplifying DLCO to CO uptake divided by alveolar PCO (Nunn & Lumb, p.145). B is tempting, but high affinity does not imply rapid binding: CO combines with haemoglobin more slowly than oxygen.

stem: Which is a selective beta blocker
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Metoprolol is a relatively selective β1-adrenoceptor antagonist, preserving β2-mediated bronchodilator, vasodilator and metabolic effects at usual doses. Its selectivity is dose-related, and β2 antagonism occurs at higher doses. Propranolol and sotalol are nonselective β1/β2 antagonists, while labetalol blocks α1-, β1- and β2-adrenoceptors (Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.494; Evers, p.699–701).

stem: When does maximal vasodilation occur after an induction dose of 1 mg/kg of propofol?
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Maximal vasodilation occurs approximately 5 minutes after the propofol bolus. The haemodynamic effect therefore lags behind loss of consciousness, which follows rapid blood–brain equilibration. Propofol lowers systemic vascular resistance by relaxing vascular smooth muscle, primarily through inhibition of sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerve activity (Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.177). Thus maximal vasodilation is not expected at loss of consciousness, despite propofol’s fast hypnotic onset.

Noradrenaline is an important neurotransmitter in descending inhibitory pain control. Most central noradrenergic neurons originate in the locus coeruleus, whose descending projections provide most noradrenergic fibres in the spinal cord. Noradrenaline released in the superficial dorsal horn inhibits nociceptive responses via α2-adrenoceptors. In contrast, substance P facilitates nociceptive transmission, while GABA and glycine principally mediate intrinsic segmental inhibition. Foundations of Anesthesia, p.278.

stem: Which type of nerve requires the lowest minimum effective concentration to block it?

options.E: Nerve with a short length exposed to local anaesthetic

reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Small myelinated fibres, particularly B fibres, require the lowest minimum blocking concentration. In myelinated axons, at least three successive nodes of Ranvier must be blocked. Smaller fibres have shorter internodal distances, so a given exposed length includes more nodes and conduction is blocked more readily. B fibres are usually blocked first because of their intrinsic sensitivity. Unmyelinated C fibres are intrinsically more resistant despite their smaller diameter (Cousins & Bridenbaugh, pp. 57, 838).

In the Marsh model, central compartment volume V1 is 0.228 × total body weight (L). Increasing weight from 80 to 100 kg therefore increases V1 from 18.24 to 22.8 L. Because the initial bolus required to achieve a target plasma concentration is proportional to V1, the bolus increases by 25%. Marsh uses total body weight as its only covariate; ke0 is not increased by weight, while k12 remains unchanged because both CL2 and V1 scale linearly with weight (Evers, p.444).

stem: Major substrate the myocardium uses most of the time
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

The heart principally metabolizes free fatty acids, which account for up to 70% of its substrate under usual conditions (Evers, p.342). They undergo mitochondrial β-oxidation to acetyl CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle. Substrate use varies: glucose predominates after a carbohydrate load and lactate may predominate during exercise, but neither is the major substrate most of the time.

stem: Which of the following is NOT seen during dynamic exercise?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

During dynamic exercise, sympathetic vasoconstriction redistributes blood flow away from the splanchnic circulation to active skeletal muscle; therefore, splanchnic vasodilation is not seen. Active-muscle vasodilation decreases systemic vascular resistance, while increased oxygen extraction widens the arterial–venous oxygen content difference. Increased pulmonary blood flow recruits and distends pulmonary capillaries, decreasing pulmonary vascular resistance and increasing pulmonary diffusing capacity.

Source: West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 71; West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 221

The total adult CSF volume is approximately 150 mL, and CSF is formed at about 500 mL/day. Thus, the total CSF volume is replaced approximately three to four times each day. These values are stated in Guyton & Hall, p.739; Hemmings & Hopkins also gives an adult volume of 150 mL and production of 500–600 mL/day.

stem: Which is not an effect of thiazide diuretic?
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Thiazide diuretics stimulate calcium reabsorption and reduce urinary calcium excretion; they may cause hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia. They are therefore used to prevent recurrent calcium-containing renal calculi. Chronic thiazide therapy commonly causes hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, and sodium depletion may accompany kaliuresis (Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.550).

stem: During a increased sympathetic state, the main mechanism of coronary artery vasodilation

options.E: Vasodilation via increased myocardial oxygen extraction

reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and contractility, increasing myocardial metabolism and oxygen consumption. Local metabolic regulation then dilates coronary arterioles, increasing coronary blood flow approximately in proportion to myocardial oxygen demand. This indirect metabolic effect overrides the modest direct α-adrenoceptor vasoconstriction or β-adrenoceptor vasodilatation within seconds. Thus, metabolic autoregulation is the main mechanism, rather than a direct β2 effect (Guyton & Hall, pp. 254–255; Evers, p. 336).

stem: Which does not prolong the duration of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents?
reason:

Chronic carbamazepine therapy causes resistance to non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers and may shorten their duration, rather than prolong it. In contrast, gentamicin, an aminoglycoside, inhibits prejunctional acetylcholine release and depresses postjunctional nicotinic receptor sensitivity; magnesium decreases presynaptic acetylcholine release; and lignocaine can potentiate neuromuscular block. Magnesium specifically prolongs non-depolarizing block (Evers, p.953).

stem: Which of the following do Beta blockers cause

β-blockers antagonise cardiac β1-adrenoceptors, preventing catecholamine-mediated positive inotropy and thereby decreasing myocardial contractility. Propranolol reduces both heart rate and contractility (Evers, p.701). Bronchodilation is instead a β2-adrenoceptor agonist effect; non-selective β-blockade may increase airway resistance or cause bronchoconstriction.

stem: What does renin do physiologically

reason:

Ventricular myocytes are working, fast-response cardiac muscle cells with a stable phase 4 resting membrane potential of approximately −85 to −95 mV. They do not normally undergo spontaneous phase 4 depolarization and therefore cannot replace the SA node as a latent pacemaker. In contrast, the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres have spontaneous phase 4 depolarization and intrinsic firing rates (Kam & Power, p.171).

stem: What is the effect of increasing age on the cardiovascular system?
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Advancing age impairs baroreceptor mechanisms, reducing the reflex cardiovascular response to acute changes in arterial pressure and increasing susceptibility to postural hypotension (Kam & Power, p.500). In contrast, arterial compliance decreases because the large arteries stiffen; this increases systolic pressure and left ventricular afterload. Reduced β-adrenergic responsiveness also lowers, rather than increases, maximal heart rate.

Catecholamines mobilise this blood from the hepatic sinusoids by reducing hepatic venous capacitance (Kam & Power, p.261).

stem: The main purpose of autoregulation of renal blood flow is to:

options.A: Maintain a relatively constant glomerular filtration rate
options.B: Maintain oxygen delivery to the renal medulla
options.C: Maintain oxygen delivery to the renal cortex
options.D: Ensure perfusion of the juxtaglomerular apparatus
options.E: Maintain a relatively constant urine output

reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Renal blood flow is much higher than required to meet renal metabolic needs. Its autoregulation therefore primarily maintains a relatively constant glomerular filtration rate despite changes in arterial pressure, allowing precise control of water and solute excretion. Urine output is not itself autoregulated; it is also influenced by tubular reabsorption and pressure diuresis.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 324; Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 325

stem: In relation to a therapeutic protein, what does recombinant mean?

options.C: Synthesised solely by non-biological chemical methods

reason:

A recombinant therapeutic protein is produced using genetic engineering techniques. Typically, the human gene encoding the protein is transfected into a suitable expression system, such as bacterial or mammalian cells; the expressed protein is then harvested and purified for therapeutic use. Recombinant does not mean extraction from pooled biological material or human plasma, nor synthesis solely by non-biological chemical methods.

Source: Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, p. 75; Rang & Dale's Pharmacology, p. 76

stem: Reason for delayed propofol offset after a bolus dose in hypovolaemia
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Propofol bolus effect terminates predominantly as drug redistributes from the vessel-rich brain to less well-perfused muscle and fat. Hypovolaemia reduces cardiac output and tissue perfusion, slowing intercompartmental transfer and therefore redistribution; brain concentrations decline more slowly. Metabolism is rapid but is not the principal determinant of offset after a single bolus. Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.28, identifies redistribution as a substantial component of bolus offset; Evers, p.1042, describes propofol’s three-compartment behaviour.

stem: According to ALS guidelines, in management of VF arrest, what should occur after 200J shock

Adrenaline and amiodarone are used later in the algorithm for persistent or refractory VF, not immediately after the initial shock. Stoelting’s Pharmacology & Physiology, p.890, identifies effective chest compressions and defibrillation as the key measures for achieving ROSC.

stem: Mechanism of Valsalva terminating SVT is:

options.B: Hypertension after cessation of intrathoracic pressure

Results under equilibrium experimental conditions may differ and should not be used to infer the clinical sequence.

stem: What is ketamine least likely to do?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Ketamine is least likely to inhibit the laryngeal reflex because upper airway reflexes remain relatively intact, with upper airway skeletal muscle tone maintained. It increases pulmonary vascular resistance, may increase muscle tone, and increases salivary and tracheobronchial secretions. Ventilation is not significantly depressed and the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide is maintained, although breathing frequency typically decreases transiently for 2–3 minutes after administration.

Source: Foundations of Anesthesia (Hemmings & Hopkins), p. 304; Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology, p. 205

stem: When is flow highest in PCV?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

In pressure-controlled ventilation, inspiratory pressure rises rapidly to the set level. The pressure gradient between the ventilator and alveoli is therefore greatest at the beginning of inspiration, producing peak inspiratory flow. As the alveoli fill, alveolar pressure rises toward airway pressure, reducing the pressure gradient and causing a decelerating inspiratory flow pattern. At end-inspiration, when airway and alveolar pressures equilibrate, flow approaches zero.

Source: West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 232; West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 231

stem: What happens in stage 1 Valsalva ?
reason:
Explanation written by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-10 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

In phase I, the onset of straining raises intrathoracic pressure. This pressure is transmitted to the aorta and displaces blood from the pulmonary circulation into the left atrium. Left ventricular filling and stroke volume therefore increase transiently, causing a brief rise in arterial blood pressure. The baroreceptor response produces a brief fall, rather than an increase, in heart rate.

Source: West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 231

Coronary blood flow increases 3- to 4-fold; the exercise table shows an increase from 250 mL/min at rest to 1000 mL/min during heavy exercise. Therefore, “more than triples” is the single best answer. An increase of only 50% substantially underestimates this response.

stem: What does velocity time integral represent?
reason:
Explanation written and 1 distractor(s) added by the tracker's GPT generator (gpt-5.6-sol, prescribed-text grounded), 2026-09-08 — the key is unchanged and not examiner-verified.

Velocity–time integral is the integral of velocity with respect to time, equivalent to the area under the velocity–time waveform. Its units are distance/time × time = distance, usually expressed in cm. It therefore represents the distance travelled by blood during the measured period. It is not flow: flow has units of volume per unit time, and equals velocity multiplied by cross-sectional area (Guyton & Hall, p.164).

stem: Compared with air, the principal physical property of heliox responsible for reducing turbulent airway resistance is:

Heliox has a substantially lower density than air because helium replaces nitrogen in the inspired gas. Lower gas density reduces the Reynolds number and therefore the tendency for turbulent flow. Because resistance during turbulent flow is density-dependent, heliox reduces airway resistance, particularly in the large airways where turbulence is most likely. Decreased viscosity is not responsible; higher, rather than lower, viscosity makes turbulence less likely.

Source: West's Respiratory Physiology, p. 232

stem: In obesity which volume is least affected

Tidal volume is least affected by obesity. With the exception of tidal volume, obesity reduces all static lung volumes, particularly expiratory reserve volume and consequently functional residual capacity. Increased intra-abdominal pressure and the weight of abdominal contents displace the diaphragm cephalad, reducing thoracic volume; these effects are greater when supine. Inspiratory reserve volume is therefore also reduced, whereas resting tidal volume is relatively preserved (Nunn & Lumb’s Respiratory Physiology, p.245).

Lung compliance increases rather than decreases because loss of elastic recoil makes the lung more distensible (Stoelting, p.878). In healthy ageing, PaCO2 is generally maintained by regulation of alveolar ventilation.

However, right atrial pressure relative to intrathoracic pressure—the transmural pressure relevant to cardiac filling—decreases at higher PEEP. The resulting reduction in right ventricular filling reduces right ventricular stroke volume, left ventricular filling and cardiac output.

Source: Nunn & Lumb's Respiratory Physiology, p. 474; Nunn & Lumb's Respiratory Physiology, p. 472
